topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
scope_note: General, mainstream workplace/management-training practice for giving feedback to peers or reports in everyday one-to-ones and reviews. Not a clinical, therapeutic, or formal HR/disciplinary process, and not tied to one named empirical study.

facts.statement: A widely taught way to structure workplace feedback is in three parts, in this order: name a specific behaviour, describe its concrete impact, then ask a question that invites the other person's view.
facts.caveat: Different training programs name the parts differently and some add a fourth part (such as a situation or context statement), but the behaviour, then impact, then question order is a common simplification taught across many of them.

facts.statement: In this context a behaviour means an observable action, such as specific words said or a specific thing done or not done, as distinct from an inferred trait, motive or label.
The first part of the feedback names a specific, observable behaviour rather than a general trait or character judgement.
facts.caveat: Keeping the description specific and observable is the widely recommended practice, though people vary in how naturally they do this.

facts.statement: Describing the concrete impact of a behaviour, such as its effect on the task, the team or the outcome, helps the other person understand why the behaviour matters rather than only that someone is unhappy.
facts.caveat: The exact wording of impact varies by situation; what matters is that it is concrete rather than a vague feeling.

facts.statement: Feedback directed at a person's character rather than their behaviour, such as calling someone disorganized rather than describing what they did, is commonly heard as a judgement of identity and tends to trigger defensiveness.
facts.caveat: This is a common tendency described in management training, not a universal law that applies identically to every person or culture.

facts.statement: Vague feedback, such as telling someone to communicate better without naming what they said or did, does not identify which specific action to repeat, change or stop.

Because vague or character-directed feedback does not identify a specific, repeatable action, it tends not to change what the person does the next time a similar situation comes up, even when it changes how they feel in the moment.
facts.caveat: This is a general pattern described in workplace feedback guidance, not a measured statistic; results vary by relationship and context.

facts.statement: Ending feedback with a question, rather than only stating a conclusion, invites the other person to add context, agree or disagree with the impact described, and take part in deciding what happens next.
A closing question that asks what the other person noticed, what they think happened, or what might help next time, turns the exchange into a two-way conversation rather than a one-way verdict.

A well known workplace feedback framework with a similar structure is Situation, Behavior, Impact, often called SBI, which is used in many leadership and management training programs and names the situation, the specific behaviour, and its impact.
facts.caveat: SBI itself does not prescribe ending with a question; it is one of several similar behaviour-and-impact frameworks taught under different names, and this lesson's behaviour, impact, question shape is a simplified, common pattern rather than a single standardized model.
facts.reference_hint: Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) feedback model, commonly associated with Center for Creative Leadership training materials

facts.statement: Giving feedback close in time to the specific behaviour, using a recent and concrete example, makes it easier for the other person to recall exactly what happened and connect the feedback to that moment.
facts.caveat: No fixed time limit (such as a number of hours or days) is established as a rule; sooner and more concrete is the general guidance.

facts.statement: A feedback conversation that only states a verdict, such as telling someone what they need to do without checking their perspective, can feel one-sided to the receiver even when the content is accurate.
Inviting the other person's view before agreeing on a next step increases the chance that the agreed change is something they understand and can actually do differently.
facts.caveat: This reflects general workplace-feedback and coaching guidance rather than a specific measured outcome.

facts.statement: Keeping the subject of the feedback sentence as the behaviour, such as what was said or done, rather than the person, helps the receiver treat the conversation as being about an action that can change rather than about who they are.

not_claimed: A fixed ideal ratio of positive to negative feedback (such as a 3-to-1 or similar ratio, sometimes called the positivity or Losada ratio) that reliably produces behaviour change; this specific ratio claim has been challenged and is not used here.
Learning-styles or VARK matching (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) makes feedback land better or change behaviour faster; the meshing hypothesis behind this is unsupported.
Any precise percentage or statistic about how many feedback conversations succeed, fail, or change behaviour; no verifiable, named source for such a figure is used here.
A single universally agreed timing rule, such as feedback must be given within a specific number of hours or days, that applies to every situation.
The 'feedback sandwich' (praise, then criticism, then praise) as a scientifically validated best practice; evidence on it is mixed and it is not relied on in this lesson.
Any claim attributed to a specific named real company, real named individual, or a specific cited study; the practices here are described as common, general workplace guidance.
